answers.text: Three lines, always the same order — drop-off time, pallet count, damage noted. If there's no damage, I'd still write 'none' rather than leave the line blank.
List each call by time, customer, topic and outcome, then count how many need a follow-up. If someone calls twice about the same thing, I'd only count it once.
The finish time doesn't work — an 8am start for six hours should wrap up early afternoon the same day, not the next. I'd check the log for the real finish time.
96 to 118 looks bigger than a 20% rise to me. The on-time rate might need a second look too.
Output 2 — it shows the 940 and 827 behind the 88%. Output 1 might be right too, but there's nothing to check it against.
Email 2, it has the real volume numbers, 1,200 to 1,650. Email 1 doesn't say what it's comparing against, so there's nothing to verify.
1. No. 2. Yes. 3. No. 4. No, still cautious with an unvetted tool. 5. No.
I'd redact the hourly rates, and I'd flag the non-disclosure clause since it names both parties. The general service scope seems fine to paste as is.
Before the summary goes out, I'd cross-check the stock counts against the system.
Step 1 matters because a bad read carries through, and step 4 — automatic submission — is where I'd want the real gate.
